newsitem.title: UK: UK exporters' worry deepens as pound piles on pain.
newsitem.headline: UK exporters' worry deepens as pound piles on pain.

text.p: Sterling's relentless rise against the German mark continued to pile on the pain for British exporters this week, raising fears of fresh cuts in earnings forecasts and the spectre of job cuts.
Britain's currency hit a 52-month high against the mark on Tuesday to flirt with levels reached when it left the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992.
Forty percent of British corporate profits come from overseas.

But as the Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang sought to play down the issue, saying exports were still possible with a strong pound, companies warned it was cutting profits and could threaten jobs.

Mike Young, director of European investment strategy at Goldman Sachs, told Reuters "There is a hope among companies that the pound's gain is temporary. But if it's sustained, that would ultimately translate into lower employment growth and job cuts."
That view was backed by British Steel which has seen its profit forecasts for the year to March 1998 halved from around 650 million pounds on the sterling factor alone.

"If this continues into April, May or June -- then it will really start to bite. Cost efficiency procedures will have to accelerate and that will have an impact on jobs," said a spokesman for the steel giant.
More recently, food and drinks group Allied Domecq predicted on Tuesday a 20 million sterling impact on its annual profits.
Reuters Holdings Plc chief executive Peter Job said on the same day in its results statement that "a robust sterling would severely restrict prospects for reported revenue and earnings growth."

Building material companies with big operations in Germany, including Redland Plc and BPB Plc, have warned of a potentially major impact on their profits, demonstrating the scale of the problem across British industry.

The Confederation of British Industry warned last week the pound was a worry. Sudhir Junankar, the CBI's director of economic analysis, told Reuters on Wednesday the currency's strength could force companies to seek cost efficiencies elsewhere.
He said the worst hit sectors to date were chemicals, textiles and metal products, with food, drink and tobacco companies partly cushioned by strong demand at home.

Robert Barrie, chief European equity economist at BZW, said: "A whole raft of corporate sectors export to Europe. This means there is a depressing earnings outlook for the UK market which still has further downgrades still to come."
Barrie predicts that sterling could depress the overall return for the British equities market to eight percent, or even lower if there is not a downward correction in the pound soon.
Goldman's Young said "Our estimates say that every 10 percent appreciation of sterling against its trade weighted index leads to a four percent drop in earnings over a full year."
The ascent of the pound began last year. Since the start of 1996 sterling has risen 17 percent on a trade weighted basis and 25 percent against the mark. Sterling is currently trading at 2.74 marks.
Young added that the currency pain inflicted on business could boost the case for those in favour of Britain joining European economic and monetary union in 1999.
"It does strengthen the case of those arguing for a single currency. But then again, there are some who take a perverse pride in currency strength."
